  "questions": [
    {
      "type": "mcq",
      "difficulty": 1,
      "stem": "What represents the instantaneous velocity on a position-versus-time graph at a given point?",
      "options": [
        "The slope of the tangent line at that point",
        "The area under the curve",
        "The total distance traveled divided by the total time",
        "The slope of the secant line over a finite time interval"
      ],
      "correct_option": 0,
      "misconceptions": [
        "",
        "confuses instantaneous velocity with the integral of position",
        "confuses instantaneous velocity with average speed over the whole trip",
        "confuses instantaneous velocity with average velocity over a finite time interval"
      ],
      "answer": "The slope of the tangent line at that point",
      "key_points": [],
      "formula": "",
      "variables": [],
      "value": 0,
      "unit": "",
      "explanation": "On a position-versus-time graph, the instantaneous velocity at any specific time is defined geometrically as the slope of the tangent line to the curve at that point. Secant lines represent average velocities over finite time intervals rather than the instantaneous value. Review the definition of instantaneous velocity from position-time graphs.",
      "sources": [
        "S7"
      ]
    },
    {
      "type": "mcq",
      "difficulty": 2,
      "stem": "If a particle moves along the x-axis with a velocity of $-7.0 \\text{ m/s}$ and another particle moves along the same axis with a velocity of $+7.0 \\text{ m/s}$, how do their instantaneous speeds compare?",
      "options": [
        "They have different speeds because their directions are opposite",
        "Both have the same speed of $7.0 \\text{ m/s}$",
        "The particle with $-7.0 \\text{ m/s}$ has a negative speed",
        "The particle with $+7.0 \\text{ m/s}$ has a higher speed"
      ],
      "correct_option": 1,
      "misconceptions": [
        "thinks speed includes directional information like velocity",
        "",
        "assumes speed can be negative when velocity is negative",
        "thinks positive velocity implies a greater magnitude than negative velocity"
      ],
      "answer": "Both have the same speed of $7.0 \\text{ m/s}$",
      "key_points": [],
      "formula": "",
      "variables": [],
      "value": 0,
      "unit": "",
      "explanation": "Instantaneous speed is the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity, meaning it is always a non-negative scalar value.       "sources": [
        "S6"
      ]
    },
    {
      "type": "mcq",
      "difficulty": 3,
      "stem": "Consider the motion of a particle with position function $x(t) = (3.0 \\text{ m/s})t - (3 \\text{ m/s}^2)t^2$. What is the instantaneous velocity at $t = 0.50 \\text{ s}$?",
      "options": [
        "$-3.0 \\text{ m/s}$",
        "$0.0 \\text{ m/s}$",
        "$1.5 \\text{ m/s}$",
        "$3.0 \\text{ m/s}$"
      ],
      "correct_option": 1,
      "misconceptions": [
        "uses incorrect differentiation or arithmetic signs",
        "",
        "calculates only the first term without subtracting the derivative of the second term",
        "forgets to multiply the time by the acceleration term's coefficient"
      ],
      "answer": "$0.0 \\text{ m/s}$",
      "key_points": [],
      "formula": "",
      "variables": [],
      "value": 0,
      "unit": "",
      "explanation": "The instantaneous velocity is the derivative of the position function with respect to time: $v(t) = \\frac{dx}{dt} = 3.0 - 6.0t$. Substituting $t = 0.50 \\text{ s}$ yields $v(0.50) = 3.0 - 6.0(0.50) = 3.0 - 3.0 = 0.0 \\text{ m/s}$. Be careful to apply the power rule correctly when differentiating polynomial position functions.",
      "sources": [
        "S1"
      ]
    },
    {
      "type": "short",
      "difficulty": 2,
      "stem": "Explain how average velocity relates to instantaneous velocity as the time interval $\\Delta t$ becomes smaller and approaches zero on a position-time graph.",
      "options": [],
      "correct_option": -1,
      "misconceptions": [],
      "answer": "As the time interval $\\Delta t$ approaches zero, the secant line representing average velocity converges to the tangent line at a specific point, meaning the average velocity approaches the instantaneous velocity at that point.",
      "key_points": [
        "Average velocity is the slope of a secant line over a finite time interval.",
        "As $\\Delta t \\to 0$, the time interval shrinks around a specific point.",
        "The average velocity approaches the slope of the tangent line, which is the instantaneous velocity."
      ],
      "formula": "",
      "variables": [],
      "value": 0,
      "unit": "",
      "explanation": "Average velocity is calculated over a time interval $\\Delta t$ as the slope of a secant line connecting two points. When you shrink $\\Delta t$ towards zero, the two points merge into a single point, turning the secant line into a tangent line whose slope is the instantaneous velocity. Review how secant lines transition to tangent lines on $x$-$t$ graphs.",
      "sources": [
        "S4",
        "S5",
        "S7"
      ]
    },
    {
      "type": "numeric",
      "difficulty": 3,
      "stem": "A particle's position is given by $x(t) = (3.0 \\text{ m/s})t + (0.5 \\text{ m/s}^3)t^3$. Calculate the instantaneous velocity at $t = 2.0 \\text{ s}$.",
      "options": [],
      "correct_option": -1,
      "misconceptions": [],
      "answer": "The instantaneous velocity at $t = 2.0 \\text{ s}$ is $9.0 \\text{ m/s}$.",
      "key_points": [],
      "formula": "3.0 + 1.5 * t**2",
      "variables": [
        {
          "name": "t",
          "value": 2.0
        }
      ],
      "value": 9.0,
      "unit": "m/s",
      "explanation": "To find the instantaneous velocity, take the derivative of the position function: $v(t) = 3.0 + 1.5t^2$. Substituting $t = 2.0 \\text{ s}$ into the derivative gives $v(2.0) = 3.0 + 1.5(2.0)^2 = 3.0 + 1.5(4.0) = 9.0 \\text{ m/s}$. Double-check your differentiation rules for polynomial exponents.",
      "sources": [
        "S2"
      ]
    },
    {
      "type": "numeric",
      "difficulty": 4,
      "stem": "Consider a particle with position function $x(t) = (3.0 \\text{ m/s})t - (3 \\text{ m/s}^2)t^2$. Determine the instantaneous speed of the particle at $t = 1.0 \\text{ s}$.",
      "options": [],
      "correct_option": -1,
      "misconceptions": [],
      "answer": "The instantaneous speed at $t = 1.0 \\text{ s}$ is $3.0 \\text{ m/s}$.",
      "key_points": [],
      "formula": "abs(3.0 - 6.0 * t)",
      "variables": [
        {
          "name": "t",
          "value": 1.0
        }
      ],
      "value": 3.0,
      "unit": "m/s",
      "explanation": "First, find the instantaneous velocity by taking the derivative: $v(t) = 3.0 - 6.0t$. At $t = 1.0 \\text{ s}$, the velocity is $v(1.0) = 3.0 - 6.0(1.0) = -3.0 \\text{ m/s}$. Speed is the magnitude of velocity, so we take the absolute value to get $|-3.0 \\text{ m/s}| = 3.0 \\text{ m/s}$. Remember that speed is always non-negative.",
      "sources": [
        "S1",
        "S6"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
